answer:
As at 2026-11-06, the Advance Medical Directive Act 1996 (the "Act") allows the following person to make an advance medical directive ("directive"):

**Who may make one**

- A person who is **not mentally disordered** [CITE:1]
- A person who has **attained 21 years of age** [CITE:1]
- A person who **desires not to be subjected to extraordinary life-sustaining treatment** in the event of suffering from a terminal illness [CITE:1]

Such a person may make a directive **at any time**, in the prescribed form; the person does not need to be terminally ill at the time of making it, since the refusal of treatment is directed at a future event of terminal illness [CITE:1].

The Act's own definition of "patient" tracks the same three requirements: not mentally disordered, at least 21 years old, and having made or desiring to make a directive in accordance with the Act [CITE:7].

**Terms that matter**

- "**Extraordinary life-sustaining treatment**" means any medical procedure or measure which, when administered to a terminally ill patient, will only prolong the process of dying when death is imminent, but it excludes palliative care [CITE:7].
- "**Palliative care**" includes reasonable medical procedures for the relief of pain, suffering or discomfort, and the reasonable provision of food and water [CITE:7].
- "**Terminal illness**" means an incurable condition caused by injury or disease from which there is no reasonable prospect of a temporary or permanent recovery, where death would be imminent within reasonable medical judgment regardless of extraordinary life-sustaining treatment, and such treatment would only postpone the moment of death [CITE:7].

**Formalities attached to making the directive**

- The directive must be made in the prescribed form and must be witnessed by two witnesses present at the same time: one must be the patient's family medical practitioner or another practitioner of the patient's choice, and the other must be a person aged 21 or above [CITE:1].
- Each witness must, to the best of their knowledge, not be a beneficiary under the patient's will or any insurance policy, have no interest under any instrument under which the patient is donor, settlor or grantor, have no entitlement to an interest in the patient's estate on intestacy or in the patient's Central Provident Fund or other provident fund monies on death, and not have registered an objection under section 10(1) [CITE:1].
- Before witnessing execution, a witness who is a medical practitioner must take reasonable steps to ensure that the patient is not mentally disordered, has attained 21 years of age, has made the directive voluntarily and without inducement or compulsion, and has been informed of the nature and consequences of making the directive [CITE:13].
- The directive must be registered with the Registrar, and a person must not act on a directive that has not been registered [CITE:2].

**Related safeguards**

- A patient who is conscious and capable of exercising rational judgment must still be informed of the various forms of treatment available so that the patient can make an informed judgment, and the Act does not affect the patient's right to decide on the use of extraordinary life-sustaining treatment while able to do so [CITE:12].
- The Act does not affect any person's right to refuse medical or surgical treatment [CITE:18].
- Where a person is charged with procuring a directive by deception, fraud, misstatement, unconscionable conduct or undue influence, falsifying or forging a directive, or wilfully concealing a revocation, no person may act on the directive unless it is ascertained that it was validly and voluntarily made, and a conviction deems the directive revoked and of no effect [CITE:16].
- The Act does not apply to any act done or any directive or instrument made or executed before 1 July 1997 [CITE:10].

answer:
**As at 2026-11-06, the normal deadline is 6 months from the date on which representation in regard to the deceased's estate is first taken out** — that is, from the date the grant of probate or letters of administration over the estate was first obtained, rather than from the date of death [CITE:1][CITE:11]. This is the rule in section 4(1) of the Inheritance (Family Provision) Act 1966, and it applies to applications for an order that reasonable provision be made for the maintenance of a "dependant", meaning a surviving spouse, an unmarried daughter (or one disabled by mental or physical disability), an infant son, or a son disabled by mental or physical disability [CITE:4].

In working out when representation was first taken out, a grant limited to trust property is left out of account unless a grant limited to the remainder of the estate has previously been made or is made at the same time [CITE:1].

**The six months is not an absolute bar.** The court may extend the period if satisfied that the limit would operate unfairly in consequence of: (a) discovery of a will or codicil involving a substantial change in the disposition of the estate; (b) a question as to whether a person had an interest in the estate, or as to the nature of that interest, not having been determined when representation was first taken out; or (c) some other circumstances affecting the administration or distribution of the estate [CITE:1].

Personal representatives who distribute the estate after the six months have expired are not rendered liable merely because the court might later extend the period, although any power to recover what was so distributed survives if an order is made [CITE:1].

**Applications made after the period has expired** (including any extension) are dealt with under section 6, which permits the court to make an order only in limited situations: varying a previous order because a material fact was not disclosed or because of a substantial change in the circumstances of the dependant or of a person beneficially interested in the property, or making provision for the maintenance of another dependant — and then only as respects property the income of which is at that date applicable for the maintenance of a dependant [CITE:5].

Finally, the Act does not apply at all to the estates of deceased Muslims, whose estates are instead distributed under Muslim law [CITE:2][CITE:9].

[CITE:2] This is not an automatic fixed share: the court decides what constitutes reasonable provision in the circumstances. [CITE:2]

answer:
As at 2026-11-06, the Maintenance of Parents Act 1995 (Singapore) permits the following persons or bodies to apply to the Tribunal for a maintenance order against one or more children of a parent [CITE:3][CITE:19].

### 1. The parent

A person may apply personally if the person:

- is domiciled and resident in Singapore;
- is at least 60 years old; and
- is unable to maintain himself or herself adequately.

The order may require one or more children to pay a monthly allowance, another periodic payment, or a lump sum [CITE:3]. “Unable to maintain adequately” means that the person’s total or expected income and other financial resources are inadequate to provide basic amenities and basic physical needs, including shelter, food, medical costs and clothing [CITE:3].

The age requirement does not automatically exclude a younger person: the Act applies if the Tribunal is satisfied that the person has an infirmity of mind or body that prevents or makes it difficult for the person to maintain himself or herself, or that there is any other special reason [CITE:3].

### 2. An approved person or organisation caring for the parent

An approved person or organisation in whose care the parent resides may apply for an order requiring one or more of the parent’s children to pay the approved person or organisation for the purpose of defraying the costs and expenses of maintaining the parent [CITE:3].

### 3. The Commissioner for the Maintenance of Parents

The Commissioner may make an application on behalf of a parent aged 60 or above, whether or not the parent is able to make the application personally, and may represent the parent in proceedings or an appeal [CITE:19]. The Commissioner may also act for a parent below 60 if satisfied that the parent has an infirmity of mind or body preventing or making maintenance difficult, or if there is any other special reason [CITE:19].

### Referral and permission requirements

Where a person other than the Commissioner intends to make a new application, either on their own behalf or on behalf of a parent, the claim must first be referred to the Commissioner if no application had previously been made in respect of that claim [CITE:3]. If the claim remains unsettled after the Commissioner’s referral, conciliation or other measures, an application may then be made to the Tribunal [CITE:19].

Permission under section 3B must first be obtained where the parent has a record or purported record of abandoning, abusing or neglecting the child and the specified trigger applies, such as a relevant declaration, notification or ascertainment by the Commissioner, or discontinuance of conciliation [CITE:6]. Permission may be granted if there is a good arguable case that the parent did not abandon, abuse or neglect the child, or that the child should maintain the parent on just and equitable grounds [CITE:6].

These provisions govern who may apply; an order is not automatic. The Tribunal must be satisfied that maintenance should be ordered on just and equitable grounds and must consider the statutory financial and other circumstances [CITE:2].

answer:
I could not find strong, comprehensive authority for this question in the material available to me; the answer below is limited to the statutory provisions actually reproduced in the sources, which themselves direct you to check Singapore Statutes Online for the latest version. [CITE:1]

**As at 2026-11-06, on the facts you state — you are 19 years old and married — you do not need your parents' or guardian's permission for sterilisation under the Voluntary Sterilisation Act 1974 (Singapore).** [CITE:1]

### Why your own consent is enough

- The Act makes it lawful for a registered medical practitioner to carry out treatment for sexual sterilisation, subject to sections 3 and 4. [CITE:1] [CITE:10]
- For a **married person below 21 years of age**, the statutory condition is that **the person consents** to the treatment, subject only to the capacity-related exception discussed below. [CITE:1]
- A parent's consent is required only in the different case of an **unmarried** person below 21, who must consent together with at least one parent or guardian. [CITE:1]
- If you are **21 or older**, your own consent is likewise sufficient, whether married or unmarried. [CITE:1]

### The capacity exception

- If you are a married person who lacks capacity within the meaning of section 4 of the Mental Capacity Act 2008 to consent, the treatment may be carried out only if, on your spouse's application, the court makes an order declaring that the treatment is necessary in your best interests. [CITE:1]
- Part 2 of the Mental Capacity Act 2008 applies, with necessary modifications, for determining both capacity and best interests for this purpose. [CITE:1] "Court" here means the General Division of the High Court or a Family Court. [CITE:3]

### Other conditions that do apply

- **Explanation and certification:** before the treatment, the practitioner must give you a full and reasonable explanation of its meaning and consequences, and you must certify that you clearly understand them. [CITE:1]
- **Place and practitioner:** the treatment must be carried out only in a health institution and by a registered medical practitioner authorised by the person having the management or control of that institution. [CITE:10] If the institution is a specialist medical clinic, the practitioner must also possess the prescribed surgical or obstetric qualifications. [CITE:10] A "health institution" includes approved permanent premises licensed to provide an acute hospital service or ambulatory surgical centre service, or a specialist medical clinic. [CITE:3]
- **Scope of the term:** "treatment for sexual sterilisation" means the surgical sterilisation of a male or female that does not involve removal of the reproduction glands or organs unless the removal is necessary for medical or therapeutic reasons. [CITE:3] The sources provided do not address non-surgical contraceptive methods, which are outside this definition. [CITE:3]

### Related protections

- It is an offence for any person, by coercion or intimidation, to compel or induce another person to undergo sterilisation against that person's will, punishable by a fine of up to $10,000, imprisonment of up to 5 years, or both. [CITE:6]
- No person is under any duty, by contract or by any statutory or legal requirement, to participate in sterilisation to which they have a conscientious objection. [CITE:5]
- A registered medical practitioner is not civilly or criminally liable for carrying out the treatment so long as the section 3(2) conditions are satisfied and the treatment is not carried out in a negligent manner. [CITE:8] Treatment by a registered medical practitioner does not constitute grievous hurt under section 320 of the Penal Code 1871. [CITE:12]
- Information about the treatment is protected: a person concerned with the medical records or participating in the treatment must not disclose facts or information about it unless you expressly consent, except as prescribed; breach is an offence. [CITE:4]

One limitation to note: the extract of section 3(5) in the sources is cut off mid-sentence, so the precise penalty provision for carrying out treatment without satisfying the section 3(2) conditions is not shown in the material available. [CITE:1]

As at 2026-11-06, the central offence is in section 5 of the Termination of Pregnancy Act 1974 (TPA), which applies to any person who, by means of coercion or intimidation, compels or induces a pregnant woman against her will to undergo treatment to terminate pregnancy [CITE:1].

## Punishment for coercing or intimidating a woman into an abortion

Under section 5 of the TPA, the offence is punishable on conviction by a fine not exceeding $3,000, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding 3 years, or both [CITE:1].

The Court of Appeal explained the policy behind these provisions: section 3(1) makes it clear that the choice to terminate a pregnancy is one for the pregnant woman alone to make, and this is reinforced by section 5, which makes it an offence for a person to compel or induce a pregnant woman to undergo treatment to terminate pregnancy [CITE:9].

## Where the pressure takes the form of a threat

If the threat amounts to the offence of criminal intimidation, section 506 of the Penal Code applies [CITE:18].

Under the ordinary form of that offence, the punishment is imprisonment for a term which may extend to 2 years, or a fine, or both [CITE:18].

The aggravated form applies where the threat is to cause death or grievous hurt, to cause the destruction of any property by fire, or to cause an offence punishable with death or with imprisonment for a term which may extend to 7 years or more, and carries imprisonment for a term which may extend to 10 years, or a fine, or both [CITE:18].

The extract provided does not reproduce the elements of criminal intimidation, so whether a particular threat falls within section 506 cannot be determined from these sources [CITE:18].

## Offences that may arise if the woman is made to undergo the abortion

If a pregnancy is terminated in circumstances where the woman did not consent, the Penal Code provides for several separate offences, depending on what occurred.

Causing a miscarriage generally is punishable by imprisonment for a term which may extend to 3 years, or a fine, or both, and if the pregnancy was of more than 16 weeks' duration, by imprisonment for a term which may extend to 7 years and a fine [CITE:4].

Where the woman’s consent is absent, the offence is punishable by imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for a term which may extend to 10 years, with liability to fine if imprisonment for life is not imposed [CITE:3].

Where an act intended to cause the miscarriage causes the woman’s death, the punishment is imprisonment for a term which may extend to 10 years and a fine, and if the act was done without her consent, imprisonment for life or the punishment just described, with the added point that it is not essential for the offence that the offender knew the act was likely to cause death [CITE:5].

Causing the death of a quick unborn child by an act that would amount to culpable homicide if it caused a person’s death is punishable by imprisonment for a term which may extend to 10 years and a fine [CITE:8].

Destroying the life of a child capable of being born alive is punishable by imprisonment for a term not exceeding 10 years, or a fine, or both, unless the act was immediately necessary to save the life of the mother, with 28 weeks’ or more of pregnancy being prima facie evidence of such a child [CITE:10].

For the 16-week threshold in section 312, the duration of pregnancy is calculated from the first day of the last normal menstruation of the pregnant woman to the end of the relevant week, or may be ascertained by clinical examination [CITE:14].

## Related offences where the pressure involved other conduct

Kidnapping or abducting a woman with intent that she may be compelled to marry against her will, or in order that she may be forced or seduced to illicit intercourse or to a life of prostitution, is punishable by imprisonment for a term which may extend to 10 years and a fine or caning [CITE:7].

Compelling or intimidating another person to undergo sexual sterilisation against that person’s will is punishable by a fine not exceeding $10,000, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding 5 years, or both [CITE:17].

## Procedure

Under the First Schedule to the Criminal Procedure Code 2010, the offences under sections 312, 313, 314, 315 and 316 of the Penal Code are not bailable, the police may ordinarily arrest without a warrant, a warrant ordinarily issues in the first instance, and these offences may be tried in the District Court [CITE:16].

## The lawful route to a termination

A person is not guilty of an offence under the law relating to abortion where the pregnancy is terminated by an authorised medical practitioner acting on the request of the pregnant woman and with her written consent [CITE:6].

Except as provided for in section 10 of the TPA, every treatment to terminate pregnancy must be carried out by an authorised medical practitioner in an approved institution [CITE:6].

Termination is not permitted once the pregnancy is more than 24 weeks’ duration unless it is immediately necessary to save the life or to prevent grave permanent injury to the physical or mental health of the pregnant woman, and between 16 and 24 weeks it is permitted only if carried out by an authorised medical practitioner with the prescribed qualifications or special skill [CITE:14].

The sources provided do not set out any defence or excuse to the section 5 offence, nor the elements of criminal intimidation, so those points would need to be checked in the full text of the Termination of Pregnancy Act 1974 and the Penal Code 1871 on Singapore Statutes Online [CITE:1][CITE:18].

judge_note: Full s 4 test, permanent or temporary
answer:
As at 2026-11-06, the Mental Capacity Act 2008 (Singapore) sets out the test in sections 3, 4 and 5; the copies provided are the consolidated versions stated to be in force from 9 March 2025, and the published copies direct readers to check Singapore Statutes Online for the latest version. [CITE:1][CITE:3][CITE:4]

### 1. The core test

A person lacks capacity in relation to a matter if, at the material time, the person is unable to make a decision for himself or herself in relation to that matter because of an impairment of, or a disturbance in the functioning of, the mind or brain. [CITE:1] The test therefore has three connected elements: inability to make the decision, a causal connection to an impairment or disturbance of the mind or brain, and an assessment made at the particular time ("the material time") rather than a general assessment of the person. [CITE:1] It does not matter whether the impairment or disturbance is permanent or temporary. [CITE:1] Capacity is assessed matter by matter: the court may make a declaration as to whether a person has or lacks capacity to make a specified decision or on specified matters, and as to the lawfulness of acts done or yet to be done in relation to that person. [CITE:5]

### 2. What "unable to make a decision" means

For section 4, a person is unable to make a decision if the person is unable to: (a) understand the information relevant to the decision; (b) retain that information; (c) use or weigh that information as part of the process of making the decision; or (d) communicate the decision, whether by talking, using sign language or any other means. [CITE:4] A person is not to be regarded as unable to understand the relevant information if the person can understand an explanation of it given in a way appropriate to the person's circumstances, such as simple language, visual aids or any other means. [CITE:4] Being able to retain the relevant information for a short period only does not prevent the person being regarded as able to make the decision. [CITE:4] The relevant information includes the reasonably foreseeable consequences of deciding one way or another, and of failing to decide. [CITE:4]

### 3. Presumptions and thresholds applied when assessing capacity

A person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that the person lacks capacity. [CITE:3] A person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision unless all practicable steps to help the person to do so have been taken without success. [CITE:3] A person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because the person makes an unwise decision. [CITE:3] In proceedings under the Act, other than proceedings for offences under the Act, any question whether a person lacks capacity must be decided on the balance of probabilities. [CITE:1]

### 4. Irrelevant factors

Lack of capacity cannot be established merely by reference to the person's age or appearance, or to a condition or aspect of the person's behaviour that might lead others to make unjustified assumptions about capacity. [CITE:1] The same exclusions apply to the separate question of best interests, which likewise must not be determined merely on the basis of age or appearance, or of such a condition or behaviour. [CITE:9]

### 5. Capacity is distinct from best interests

Even where a person is found to lack capacity, an act done or decision made under the Act for or on behalf of that person must be done or made in the person's best interests, and regard must be had to whether the purpose can be as effectively achieved in a way that is less restrictive of the person's rights and freedom of action. [CITE:3] The best-interests determination must consider all the relevant circumstances and, in particular, the factors set out in section 6, including whether the person is likely to have capacity in the matter later, encouraging participation as fully as possible, and considering the person's past and present wishes and feelings and the beliefs and values that would influence the person's decision if the person had capacity. [CITE:9] The supplied extract of section 6 is incomplete, so the full list of considerations is not reproduced here. [CITE:9]

### 6. Capacity in related statutory contexts

A person doing an act in connection with the care or treatment of another person must, before doing the act, take reasonable steps to establish whether that person lacks capacity in relation to the matter, and when doing the act reasonably believe both that the person lacks capacity and that it would be in the person's best interests. [CITE:8] A donee under a lasting power of attorney may only make decisions where the donor lacks capacity, or where the donee reasonably believes that the donor lacks capacity. [CITE:20] The court's general powers to make decisions and appoint deputies apply where a person lacks capacity in relation to matters concerning that person's personal welfare, or property and affairs. [CITE:11] Pending the determination of an application, the court may make an interim order or give directions where there is reason to believe the person lacks capacity in relation to the matter, the matter is one to which the court's powers extend, and it is in the person's best interests to act without delay. [CITE:2] Where a person is under 21 years of age, the Act's powers are not exercisable in relation to that person unless the court considers it likely that the person will still lack capacity in that respect at age 21. [CITE:1][CITE:14] "Court" is defined in the Act as the General Division of the High Court or a Family Court. [CITE:19]

### 7. Codes of practice on assessing capacity

The Minister may issue codes of practice for the guidance of persons assessing whether a person has capacity in relation to any matter, persons acting in connection with the care or treatment of another person, donees of lasting powers of attorney and deputies, and on other matters under the Act. [CITE:10] A person acting as a donee, as a deputy, in a professional capacity, or for remuneration must have regard to any relevant code. [CITE:10] If a provision of a code, or a failure to comply with one, appears relevant to a question in civil or criminal proceedings, the court must take it into account in deciding that question. [CITE:10]

As at 2026-11-06, **being very old or “acting oddly” does not automatically mean that your grandmother cannot legally make her own decisions**. [CITE:4]

Under section 5 of the Mental Capacity Act 2008, inability to make a decision is assessed by whether she is unable to:

- understand the information relevant to the decision;
- retain that information;
- use or weigh that information in making the decision; or
- communicate her decision. [CITE:4]

The test is therefore functional and relates to the particular decision, rather than merely to her age or personality. [CITE:4] The relevant information includes the reasonably foreseeable consequences of deciding or deciding not to decide. [CITE:4]

She cannot be regarded as unable to understand merely because she needs the information explained through simple language, visual aids, or another appropriate method, and brief retention of the information does not itself prevent her from being capable. [CITE:4] Thus, unusual behaviour alone is not conclusive evidence of legal incapacity. [CITE:4]

judge_note: Personal welfare and property and affairs
answer:
As at 2026-11-06, the Mental Capacity Act 2008 permits a lasting power of attorney to authorise a donee to make decisions for the donor in two broad areas: the donor’s personal welfare, including specified welfare matters, and the donor’s property and affairs, including specified financial or property matters. [CITE:3][CITE:8]

### General conditions

The donor is the person granting the authority, and the donee is the person authorised to exercise it. [CITE:8] A donee may make decisions only where the donor lacks capacity or the donee reasonably believes that the donor lacks capacity; merely acting while the donor still has decision-making capacity is not authorised. [CITE:1]

The lasting power of attorney must also have been validly created, and its authority is subject to the Mental Capacity Act 2008, including the principles in section 3 and the best-interests requirement in section 6, as well as any conditions or restrictions specified in the instrument. [CITE:3]

### Personal-welfare decisions

Where the lasting power of attorney authorises decisions about personal welfare:

- The donee may give or refuse consent to a healthcare provider carrying out or continuing treatment, including a clinical trial, only if the instrument expressly provides for that authority. [CITE:1]
- The donee may give, refuse or revoke appropriate consent under the Human Biomedical Research Act 2015 only if the instrument expressly provides for that authority. [CITE:1]
- The donee may not decide about life-sustaining treatment, even if the instrument purports to give broader authority. [CITE:1] “Life-sustaining treatment” means treatment which, in the view of another person providing healthcare, is necessary to sustain life. [CITE:8]
- The donee also may not decide about other treatment that a healthcare provider reasonably believes is necessary to prevent a serious deterioration in the donor’s condition. [CITE:1]
- The donee may authorise an act intended to restrain the donor only if the donee reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent harm to the donor and the act is a proportionate response to the likelihood and seriousness of that harm. [CITE:1] Restraint includes using or threatening force to secure an act the donor resists, or restricting the donor’s liberty of movement. [CITE:1]

### Property and financial decisions

A donee may make decisions about the donor’s property and affairs, but the lasting power of attorney does not authorise gifts unless it expressly authorises them. [CITE:2] If the express authorisation does not state the permitted value, the gifts must not be unreasonable having regard to all the circumstances, particularly the size of the donor’s estate, and the donee must have regard to the principle in section 6(7). [CITE:2]

### Court involvement

The court may determine the meaning or effect of a lasting power of attorney, give directions about decisions the donee is authorised to make, and give consent or authorisation that the donor would have had to give if the donor had capacity. [CITE:4] The court may also authorise the making of gifts that are not within section 14(3). [CITE:4]

answer:
As at 2026-11-06, based on the supplied consolidated text of the Vulnerable Adults Act 2018, section 10 permits the Director-General or a protector to remove a vulnerable adult from the place where the adult is residing or staying in the circumstances set out below. [CITE:1]

### Protective removal under section 10

The Director-General or protector must first be satisfied, on reasonable grounds, that the vulnerable adult has experienced, is experiencing, or is at risk of abuse, neglect or self-neglect. [CITE:1]

Removal must also fall within one of three alternative statutory routes: [CITE:1]

1. **The adult consents.** The vulnerable adult may consent to removal even though another person is preventing or trying to prevent the removal. [CITE:1]

2. **The adult lacks mental capacity to consent.** A mental capacity assessor must have assessed the vulnerable adult as lacking mental capacity to consent. If a donee or deputy has been appointed for that adult, the Director-General or protector may remove the adult without the donee’s or deputy’s consent. [CITE:1]

3. **The court authorises removal.** If the adult has mental capacity but refuses removal, the court may authorise the Director-General or protector to remove the adult on their application. The court must be satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the adult has experienced, is experiencing, or is at risk of abuse, neglect or self-neglect, and must consider the order necessary for the adult’s protection and safety. [CITE:1]

Thus, a capable adult’s refusal does not by itself prevent removal, because removal may instead be made under a section 10(4) court order, but the risk findings and court authorisation are still required. [CITE:1]

### Entry and use of force

For the purpose of exercising the section 10 removal power, the Director-General or protector may enter premises where the adult is residing or staying without notice at any time of day or night. They may be accompanied by relevant support persons and other persons considered necessary to assist them, and may break open doors, windows, locks or similar items with necessary assistance. [CITE:5]

Section 10 also permits the use of such force as the Director-General or protector considers necessary to remove the adult or to prevent another person obstructing the removal. [CITE:1]

### Governing principles

The Director-General and protector must have regard to the statutory principles when exercising these powers. [CITE:9]

These include protecting the adult from abuse, neglect and self-neglect; recognising that an adult with mental capacity is generally best placed to decide how to live and whether to accept assistance; considering the ascertainable views, wishes, feelings, values and beliefs of an adult lacking mental capacity; considering whether a less restrictive method can achieve the protective purpose; and treating the adult’s welfare and best interests as the first and paramount consideration. [CITE:9]

### Separate removal for assessment

Section 6 also permits removal from the adult’s place of residence or stay for the purpose of an assessment if the adult consents despite obstruction, has been assessed as lacking mental capacity to consent, or removal is in accordance with a court order under section 7(3). This is a distinct assessment-related power rather than the protective removal power under section 10. [CITE:3]

If the adult refuses assessment, the Director-General or protector is generally not required to exercise the section 6 powers, although section 7 provides exceptions where there is reason to believe the adult lacks capacity to refuse and assessment is in the adult’s best interests, or where a court order under section 7(3) applies. [CITE:4]

judge_note: Yes, s 10(1)(b); hedges on the under-aged definition
answer:
As at 2026-11-06, I could not find strong authority confirming the precise application to this exact purchase because the supplied extract does not define “under-aged person”; section 10 nevertheless directly addresses buying tobacco products for an under-aged person. [CITE:2]

**Yes, potentially.** If a 17-year-old falls within the statutory meaning of “under-aged person” and you buy cigarettes in Singapore for the purpose of giving them to your cousin, you would engage section 10(1)(b). Actually giving or furnishing the cigarettes to your cousin would also engage section 10(1)(c). Payment is irrelevant: the buying offence applies whether or not you give the cigarettes for a consideration. [CITE:2]

The stated maximum penalty for buying or acquiring a tobacco product for giving to an under-aged person is a fine not exceeding $2,500, or $5,000 for a second or subsequent conviction. The maximum for giving or furnishing the product is $500, or $1,000 for a second or subsequent conviction. [CITE:2]

A possible defence requires either reasonable grounds to believe the recipient was not under-aged **and** reasonable inquiries to ascertain that fact, or evidence purporting to show that the recipient was not under-aged which was reasonable to accept. If you knew your cousin was 17 and 17 is covered by the statutory definition, the first defence would appear inconsistent with those facts. [CITE:2]

The supplied materials do not define the age threshold for “under-aged person”, so they do not conclusively resolve that point; the current Act on Singapore Statutes Online would be the place to check that definition. [CITE:2]

The applicant may be: [CITE:1]

As at 2026-11-06, yes. Where an application under section 8 for the child’s return is pending or has been dismissed, the court may issue an injunction restraining any person from taking the child out of Singapore. [CITE:1]

As at 2026-11-06, under section 6(1) of the Public Trustee Act 1915, the Public Trustee **must** administer a small estate when all of the following conditions are met:

- A person who, in the Public Trustee’s opinion, would be entitled to apply to the court for administration of the estate applies to the Public Trustee to administer it [CITE:1]
- The estate’s **gross capital value** is proved to the Public Trustee’s satisfaction to be less than the prescribed amount [CITE:1]
- It appears to the Public Trustee that the persons beneficially entitled to the estate are persons of small means [CITE:1]

This mandatory duty is subject to the Public Trustee seeing good reason to refuse to administer the estate [CITE:1]. The supplied text does not state the numerical prescribed amount; that figure must be checked against the current rules and the latest legislation on Singapore Statutes Online [CITE:1].

As at 2026-11-06, the maximum is **four persons**. Section 6(1) of the Probate and Administration Act 1934 provides that probate or letters of administration shall not be granted to more than four persons in respect of the same property [CITE:1].

Related points under the same section:

- Where there is a minority or a life interest arising under the will, letters of administration must be granted either to a trust corporation (with or without an individual) or to not fewer than two individuals [CITE:1].
- A "trust corporation" means the Public Trustee or a corporation licensed as a trust company under the Trust Companies Act 2005 [CITE:1].
- If there is only one personal representative (who is not a trust corporation), the court may, during a beneficiary's minority or the subsistence of a life interest and until the estate is fully administered, appoint one or more additional personal representatives on the application of an interested person or of a guardian, committee or receiver [CITE:1].

Separately, where a will appoints more than one executor, probate may be granted to one or more of the persons so appointed, subject to section 6 [CITE:2].

As at 2026-11-06, under section 6(1)–(2) of the Children and Young Persons Act 1993, a person (“A”) knowingly permits a child (“B”) to be ill-treated by another person (“C”) if all three conditions are met: [CITE:1]

1. A has the **custody, charge or care** of B; [CITE:1]  
2. A **knows or has reason to believe** that B was at risk of being ill-treated by C; and [CITE:1]  
3. A **failed to take steps that A could reasonably have been expected, in A’s circumstances, to take** to protect B from that risk. [CITE:1]

In assessing the steps reasonably expected, A’s circumstances expressly include, though are not limited to, any past or present experience of A having been ill-treated by C. [CITE:1]

The test therefore concerns a known or reasonably suspected risk of ill-treatment and the failure to take reasonably expected protective steps, rather than merely failure to act without awareness of the risk. [CITE:1]

judge_note: Director-General, protector or police under s 115
answer:
As at 2026-11-06, I could not find strong, neighbour-specific authority in the supplied materials, but the general statutory notification provisions support a clear answer. [CITE:16]

Any member of the public, including a neighbour, may notify the Director-General of Social Welfare, a protector or a police officer if they know or have reason to suspect that a child or young person is in need of care or protection. [CITE:16][CITE:1]

The notification may state the facts and circumstances supporting the person’s knowledge or suspicion. [CITE:16]

Relevant grounds include a parent or guardian being unable or having neglected to provide adequate food, clothing, medical aid, lodging, care or other necessities, and a child being ill-treated or at risk of ill-treatment by a parent or guardian. [CITE:4]

The grounds also include situations where another person ill-treats or risks ill-treating the child and the parent or guardian, knowing of the ill-treatment or risk, has not protected or is unlikely or unwilling to protect the child. [CITE:4]

A parent or guardian is also deemed to neglect a child where they wilfully or unreasonably fail to provide adequate necessities in circumstances likely to cause physical pain, suffering, injury, emotional harm or injury to the child’s health or development. [CITE:12]

A person who makes a notification in good faith is protected from civil and criminal liability and cannot be treated as breaching professional ethics merely because of making the notification; a witness also cannot be compelled to disclose the notifier’s identity or produce an identifying report or document. [CITE:16]

answer:
As at 2026-11-06, under the supplied consolidated version of the Children and Young Persons Act 1993, a child is **in need of care or protection** if:

1. The child has been, is being, or is at risk of being ill-treated by a parent or guardian, and the parent or guardian has not protected, or is unlikely or unwilling to protect, the child from that ill-treatment. [CITE:2]  
2. The child suffers or is likely to suffer emotional harm because the child has been or is subject to emotional or psychological abuse by a parent or guardian. [CITE:2]

As at 2026-11-06, a medical practitioner who has reason to believe or suspect that a person they attend or treat has a **prescribed infectious disease**, or is a carrier of that disease, must **notify the Director-General of Health within the prescribed time and in the form or manner required by the Director-General**. [CITE:1]

The practitioner must also provide any other particulars required by the Director-General, insofar as they can reasonably be ascertained or are within the practitioner’s knowledge. [CITE:1]

Failure to comply with these notification requirements, or providing information known or reasonably believed to be false, is an offence. [CITE:1]

As at 2026-11-06, section 15(1) of the Infectious Diseases Act 1976 empowers the Director-General of Health to order three categories of persons to be detained and isolated in a hospital or other place [CITE:1]:

1. **Any person who is a case or an at-risk individual of an infectious disease** [CITE:1].
2. **Any class of persons mentioned in paragraph (a)** — that is, any class of people who are cases or at-risk individuals of an infectious disease [CITE:1].
3. **Any person who is suspected to be a case or an at-risk individual of an infectious disease** [CITE:1].

The power therefore extends beyond individually named persons to whole classes of people who fall within paragraph (a) [CITE:1].

The order may specify any period of detention and isolation and any conditions, as the Director-General of Health determines [CITE:1].

**Offence for non-compliance.** A person subject to an isolation order commits an offence if, without reasonable excuse, they fail to proceed to the place of isolation within the time specified in the order (or as soon as possible where no time is specified), fail to comply with a condition of the order without reasonable excuse, or leave or attempt to leave the place of isolation without the Director-General of Health's permission [CITE:1]. The failure-to-proceed limb does not apply where the person is already at the place they are ordered to be isolated in [CITE:1].

**Related provisions.**
- Section 15(2) allows the Director-General of Health to order the same three categories of persons, plus any person who has recently recovered from or been treated for an infectious disease, to remain isolated (and, if necessary, treated) in their own residence for as long as necessary for the protection of the public [CITE:1].
- Section 55 permits the Director-General of Health or an authorised Health Officer to enter, inspect and search premises and conveyances, take samples, seize substances or matters, require information and records, require destruction of food, and restrict movement of persons, animals and conveyances, in connection with an actual or suspected outbreak or with preventing spread [CITE:13][CITE:3][CITE:6].
- Under section 56, where a person defaults, enforcement measures may include causing that person to be taken to the place of isolation or ensuring they remain isolated in their own dwelling, for the period and on the conditions the Director-General of Health thinks necessary for public protection [CITE:2]; such measures may extend to entry into premises without a warrant and to the use of necessary force [CITE:2].

**Note on undefined terms.** The section as quoted here does not set out the meanings of "case" and "at-risk individual"; the source states the text is from the consolidated version in force from 1 April 2025 and that Singapore Statutes Online should be checked for the latest version and for the Act's definitions [CITE:1].

answer:
As at 2026-11-06, the supplied consolidated text supports the core rule below, but I could not find strong authority on every aspect because the regulations prescribing the periods and viral-load threshold for the undetectable-viral-load exception were not supplied. [CITE:1]

**Generally, yes.** A person who knows they have HIV infection must not engage in the sexual activity covered by section 23 unless, before it takes place, they have:

- informed the other person of the risk of contracting HIV from them; and
- obtained the other person’s voluntary agreement to accept that risk. [CITE:1]

The requirement is framed as disclosure of the **risk of contracting HIV**, rather than expressly requiring particular words such as an admission of HIV status. [CITE:1] For section 23, “sexual activity” means penetration of the vagina, anus or mouth by any part of another person’s penis, or cunnilingus. [CITE:4]

There is an exception: section 23(1) does not apply where the HIV-positive person has maintained an undetectable viral load for at least the prescribed period before the activity. [CITE:1] A presumption of maintaining an undetectable load generally requires recent and earlier recognised-laboratory tests showing undetectable results, no detectable result in between, and adherence to prescribed HIV treatment throughout the relevant period. [CITE:1] The exact prescribed periods and viral-load threshold must be checked in the regulations because they are not contained in the supplied material. [CITE:1]

As at 2026-11-06, the general answer under the Central Provident Fund legislation is **yes**, with two possible routes: [CITE:11][CITE:16]

judge_note: Commissioner of Police, purpose and prescribed information
answer:
As at 2026-11-06, the House to House and Street Collections Act 1947 requires that no collection be made unless the licensing requirements in the Act are satisfied [CITE:1]. Under the Act, a "collection" is an appeal to the public or any class of the public, made by visits from house to house, by soliciting in streets or other public places, or by both, asking for money or other property (whether or not for consideration), excluding money or property already legally due from the donors [CITE:3]. A "promoter" is a person who causes others to act as collectors for the purposes of a collection [CITE:3].

**From whom the licence must be obtained**

A person who wishes to promote a collection in Singapore applies to the **Commissioner of Police** [CITE:2]. Subject to the provisions of section 4 and to such conditions as the Commissioner thinks fit to impose, the Commissioner must grant a licence authorising the person to promote the collection for the specified purpose [CITE:2]. The licence is valid for such period as the Commissioner determines, and that period must be stated in the licence [CITE:2].

**What the application must specify**

The application must:

1. be made **in the prescribed manner** [CITE:2];
2. **specify the purpose of the collection** [CITE:2];
3. be accompanied by **the prescribed information** required for the application [CITE:2]; and
4. **specify an address within Singapore** for service on the applicant of any notice or other communication required to be served on the applicant [CITE:2].

A collection is treated as made for a particular purpose where the appeal is made in association with a representation that the money or property appealed for, or part of it, will be applied for that purpose [CITE:3].

The details of the "prescribed manner", the prescribed information, and other licensing requirements are set by regulations made under section 5, which empowers the Minister to prescribe requirements and to regulate the manner in which licensed collections are carried out and the conduct of promoters and collectors [CITE:5]. Those regulations are not included in the sources provided; they are subsidiary legislation that can be checked on Singapore Statutes Online [CITE:5].

judge_note: Licence or exemption needed; opens with an unnecessary hedge
answer:
I could not find strong authority in the provided sources for this question in its full generality, so I answer only what those sources directly support and keep the rest brief.

**As at 2026-11-06, the sources support a qualified "yes":** a private clinic that provides a licensable healthcare service must be authorised by a licence under the Healthcare Services Act 2020 or be exempt from that requirement, and it may provide that service only at permanent premises approved for it, using approved conveyances, or by an approved service delivery mode. [CITE:12] [CITE:13]

### 1. The core rule and the penalty

Section 8(1) provides that a person must not provide a licensable healthcare service unless the person is authorised to do so by a licence under the Act or is exempt from that section in relation to that service. [CITE:12] Contravention is an offence punishable on conviction by a fine not exceeding $100,000 or imprisonment for up to 2 years or both, rising to a fine not exceeding $200,000 (with imprisonment up to 2 years still available) where the person has a previous qualifying conviction. [CITE:12]

Section 9(1) separately requires a licensee not to provide a licensable healthcare service at any permanent premises in Singapore that is not an approved permanent premises for that service, using any conveyance that is not an approved conveyance, or by any other service delivery mode not approved under section 11B. [CITE:13] Breach is an offence carrying, for a first offence, a fine of up to $50,000 or up to 12 months' imprisonment or both, and, where there is a previous qualifying conviction, a fine of up to $100,000 or up to 12 months' imprisonment or both. [CITE:13]

### 2. Which services, and from when

The Second Schedule sets appointed days for licensable healthcare services provided in healthcare establishments, medical clinics and private hospitals: 3 January 2022 for blood banking, clinical laboratory, cord blood banking, nuclear medicine assay, nuclear medicine imaging and radiological services; 26 June 2023 for acute hospital, ambulatory surgical centre, assisted reproduction, community hospital, contingency care, human tissue banking, nuclear medicine, outpatient dental, outpatient medical and outpatient renal dialysis services; and 18 December 2023 for nursing home service. [CITE:8] All of these appointed days have passed, so the licensing requirement has applied to each listed category for some time. [CITE:8] [CITE:12]

### 3. Transitional position for clinics already operating

The Third Schedule provides that, subject to sub-paragraph (2), where a licensable healthcare service was provided immediately before its appointed day in premises licensed under the repealed Private Hospitals and Medical Clinics Act and any required approvals were in force, the licence and approval continue in force as if granted under the Healthcare Services Act for the period for which they had been granted under the repealed Act. [CITE:1] Such a continuing licence lasts until the earliest of the date it would have expired under the repealed Act, the date it ceases or is surrendered under section 17, or the date it is revoked under section 20. [CITE:1] From the appointed day, the repealed Act ceases to apply to that service provided in those premises. [CITE:1] Section 58 repealed the Private Hospitals and Medical Clinics Act, and section 60 applies the new Act, subject to the Third Schedule's adaptations, to services provided under licences issued before the appointed day and to applications pending immediately before it. [CITE:9] [CITE:2]

Older cases illustrate the predecessor regime rather than the current one: a private hospital licensed to provide assisted reproduction as a special care service under the repealed Act, and a clinic operating under a special licence subject to specific licensing conditions. [CITE:14] [CITE:19]

### 4. Additional approvals inside an existing licence

Even with a licence, a licensee must not provide a "specified service" — a service of a medical or healthcare nature prescribed for that licensable healthcare service — without the Director-General's approval under section 11D. [CITE:16] Breach is an offence punishable by up to $100,000 or 2 years' imprisonment or both, and up to $200,000 or 2 years' imprisonment for a second or subsequent offence. [CITE:16] The Director-General may impose general, class-specific or licence-specific conditions on granting or renewing a licence, and may by condition prohibit using approved permanent premises or approved conveyances for any service or activity that is not part of the licensable healthcare service even if incidental to it. [CITE:20] A licensee intending to stop providing a service at approved premises, to stop providing an approved specified service, or to amend other particulars in its licence must apply to the Director-General to amend the licence, and on approval the amended licence replaces the original. [CITE:10]

Applications for a licence are made to the Director-General in the form and manner required, with a non-refundable application fee if prescribed and prescribed particulars including the licensable healthcare service and details of the approvals sought for permanent premises, conveyances, other service delivery modes and specified services. [CITE:17]

### 5. Other licensing regimes may still apply

The Healthcare Services Act is not the only regime: a person must not use any building, situation or place as a private market without first obtaining a licence from the Director-General, Food Administration. [CITE:5] Separately, the Poisons Act exemption for a medicine supplied by a medical practitioner for the treatment of that practitioner's own patients is expressed to be subject to any rules made under that Act. [CITE:6]

### 6. A point on the sources' currency

The Healthcare Services Act text supplied is a consolidated version stated to be in force from 2023-12-18, and the source itself directs readers to check Singapore Statutes Online for the latest version, so amendments may have occurred since then. [CITE:12] On the Voluntary Sterilisation Act, the earlier source shows the 2023 amendment to the definition of "health institution", while the later consolidated text in force from 5 December 2025 shows definitions keyed to "approved permanent premises" approved for acute hospital, ambulatory surgical centre, outpatient medical and related services, so the later wording is the one in force at the date of this answer. [CITE:4] [CITE:15]

### 7. What these sources do not settle

The materials provided do not include the Act's full definition of "licensable healthcare service" or its exemptions, the complete set of licence conditions, or the detailed licensing procedures, so they cannot establish whether a particular clinic and its particular activities require a licence or an exemption; the current consolidated Act on Singapore Statutes Online and, for a specific clinic, a lawyer would be the places to check. [CITE:12]

judge_note: Loss of genetic affinity recognised; contains a malformed citation marker '[CITE:129-130 as cited in CITE:8]'
answer:
As at 2026-11-06, yes. The Court of Appeal held that, in the circumstances of *ACB v Thomson Medical Pte Ltd*, the negligence caused the appellant to suffer a loss of “genetic affinity” and recognised that loss as an actionable head of damage, recoverable as general damages. [CITE:3] [CITE:7] [CITE:10]

“Genetic affinity” concerns ties arising partly from genetic relatedness and partly from their social significance, including the importance of biological lineage and familial relationships. [CITE:9] [CITE:129–130 as cited in CITE:8]

The recognition was limited in important respects. The court did not recognise loss of autonomy as a standalone head of damage; rather, autonomy was a background consideration supporting the more specific award for loss of genetic affinity. [CITE:4] [CITE:16] It also rejected claims for the child’s upkeep costs as contrary to public policy and expressly reserved whether plaintiffs in wrongful-conception or wrongful-birth cases could claim a similar loss of affinity. [CITE:7] [CITE:14]

As at 2026-11-06, the Court of Appeal held that the mother should be awarded **30% of the financial costs of raising the child** as compensation for her loss of genetic affinity, and remitted the assessment of the precise quantum of damages to the High Court. [CITE:5] The court considered that a 30% award properly reflected the seriousness of her loss and was just, equitable and proportionate in the circumstances. [CITE:5]

Two points of clarification from the judgment:

- This was framed as a **conventional sum for non-pecuniary loss** (the mother’s loss of genetic affinity), not as an award of the child’s upkeep costs; the court expressly distinguished the two, noting that the former compensates for the mother’s non-pecuniary loss while the latter compensates pecuniary expenses of raising the child. [CITE:14] [CITE:7]
- The appeal was dismissed insofar as the claim for upkeep costs as such was concerned. [CITE:12]

The court also flagged practical difficulties in the assessment remitted to the High Court, including the dependence of rearing costs on the parents’ subjective preferences (such as private education or extra-curricular classes), the difficulty distinguishing legal obligation, moral obligation and parental discretion, and the identification of a suitable cut-off date for liability. [CITE:5]

As at 2026-11-06, the position stated in the Court of Appeal's judgment in *ACB v Thomson Medical Pte Ltd & 3 Ors* [2017] SGCA 20 is that the court dismissed the claim for the costs of raising the child, but allowed the appellant to claim general damages for loss of "genetic affinity", with the quantum to be assessed by reference to principles the court laid down [CITE:4].

## 1. The two awards rest on different legal bases

An award for **loss of genetic affinity** is an award of **non-pecuniary loss** — that is, loss that is not itself measured in money — compensating the plaintiff-mother for her loss of genetic affinity [CITE:8]. "Genetic affinity" means those ties between parents and children which are partly the result of genetic relatedness and partly the result of the social significance that relatedness carries; it is what distinguishes familial ties from ties of friendship [CITE:6].

The cognisable injury is damage to the plaintiff's interest in maintaining the integrity of her reproductive plans in the specific sense of her conscious decision to have a child with her husband so as to maintain an intergenerational genetic link and preserve affinity [CITE:5]. The court described this interest as one the law should recognise and protect, and held that damage to it should sound in damages [CITE:5]. This is not merely about an "incorrect" or "undesired" genetic mix or skin tone, which the court said it categorically rejected as framing the issue [CITE:10].

An award of **upkeep costs**, by contrast, is an award of **pecuniary loss** arising from the expenses incurred in relation to raising the child [CITE:8]. The court expressly clarified that the two awards "rest on very different theoretical bases" [CITE:8].

## 2. Why the upkeep claim was refused

The court held that the upkeep claim is a head of damages that is **contrary to public policy** and should not be recognised in Singapore [CITE:15]. Full upkeep costs would amount to an indemnity for the costs of raising the child, which the court considered would not be appropriate compensation for the loss actually suffered [CITE:12]. The focus on the financial consequences of the birth is not merely inadequate but ultimately misleading, because it ignores the moral, psychological and social obligations involved in parenting and risks masking the "real loss" suffered in such a case [CITE:17]. The underlying objection is that the obligations of parenthood are incapable of being regarded by the law as loss [CITE:12].

## 3. The "real loss" that was recognised instead

The harm consists not only of the frustration of the plaintiff's **decisional autonomy** — her ability to make free choices about her reproductive life — but also of the substantive impact on her well-being, including a loss of affinity and the chance to have a family structure matching her aspirations [CITE:6]. The court was not disposed to recognise loss of autonomy as a recoverable head of damage in its own right, while recognising autonomy as an important background consideration [CITE:14].

## 4. Quantum: the child's costs are a benchmark, not a recovery

Although full upkeep costs were not recoverable, the financial costs of raising the child were "not wholly irrelevant", because absent them there would be no criterion or standard for assessing the quantum of damages; the court therefore proposed to **benchmark the eventual award as a percentage of the financial costs of raising the child** [CITE:8]. The full quantum of upkeep costs is only a benchmark, and the award should lie between two extremes: neither full upkeep costs, which would be an inappropriate indemnity, nor a merely nominal sum, which would make a mockery of the value of the interest at stake [CITE:12]. Substantial damages were to be awarded, with the facts and circumstances of the particular case being of the first importance [CITE:12]. One purpose of a non-pecuniary award is to provide solace to the claimant, and a benchmarked award would not be derisory [CITE:8].

**In short:** the distinction is one of legal theory and function — a non-pecuniary award compensating the mother for the injury to her genetic affinity with her child, as opposed to a pecuniary indemnity for the cost of raising that child, which public policy excludes in Singapore [CITE:8][CITE:12][CITE:15]. The costs of raising the child are used only as a measuring stick for the non-pecuniary award, not as a recoverable loss in themselves [CITE:8][CITE:12]. The passages provided set out this benchmarking method but do not state the percentage or the final sum awarded, so that figure cannot be given from these sources [CITE:8][CITE:12].

judge_note: Never pleaded she would have terminated
answer:
As at 2026-11-06, the abortion-based claim failed because the mother lacked the factual premise required for a **wrongful-birth claim**: she did not say that she would have terminated the pregnancy if she had been told about the mix-up in time. [CITE:11]

A wrongful-birth claim ordinarily requires that, had the mother been informed timeously of the pregnancy or the child’s condition, she would have terminated the pregnancy; it therefore concerns the wrongful prolongation of pregnancy. [CITE:14]

In this case, the mother actively wanted a child and was willing to bear the cost of raising one, although she intended the child to be conceived using her husband’s sperm. The distinction is between:

- **Questions of pure fact**, such as what was visible on an X-ray or what was detected, which the court determines without applying Bolam-Bolitho [CITE:3].
- **The doctor’s diagnosis or conclusion**, where it involves interpretation or medical opinion, which must be assessed against the reasonable standard of care understood by medical professionals and therefore remains subject to Bolam-Bolitho [CITE:3].

Accordingly, even where the alleged negligence concerns the diagnostic decision itself, without any decision about treatment or further diagnostic procedures, Bolam-Bolitho still applies [CITE:6]. The court should not prefer one body of medical opinion over another unless that opinion is shown to be logically indefensible [CITE:4].

Under its reading of *Penney*, the court may first determine a purely factual question without applying Bolam-Bolitho, such as what abnormalities were visible on cervical-smear slides. [CITE:5]

Once those facts were established, however, whether a reasonable professional should have noticed the abnormality or acted upon it involved professional judgment and opinion and remained subject to Bolam-Bolitho; *Penney* was upheld because the trial judge had correctly applied the Bolitho exception. [CITE:5]

The Court understood *Muller* in the same way: although a wrong diagnosis may involve neither a weighing of risks against benefits nor a decision to treat, it does not attract a separate diagnostic test; any diagnosis incorporating interpretation or opinion must be measured against the reasonable standard of care understood by medical professionals. [CITE:6][CITE:4]

The distinction was therefore between the factual precursor inquiry and evaluative medical judgment: the court decides what could be observed, while the professional diagnosis is assessed through Bolam-Bolitho. [CITE:4]

answer:

In *Hii Chii Kok v Ooi Peng Jin London Lucien and another* [2016] SGHC 21, the General Division of the High Court expressly found that the plaintiff was never told by the defendants that he suffered or definitely suffered from cancer or neuroendocrine cancer, and was never told that surgery was the only option he should pursue — the two matters that were alleged to have induced his consent to the Whipple Surgery. [CITE:3]

## 1. The alleged definitive cancer diagnosis was rejected

- On the balance of probabilities, the court found the plaintiff was never informed or advised by the defendants that he suffered from pancreatic cancer or neuroendocrine cancer, describing the allegation as “a bald allegation levied against the defendants by the plaintiff in a futile attempt to fortify his claim”. [CITE:5]
- The Tumour Board’s Diagnoses and Advice referred exclusively to pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (“PNETs”) and hyperplasia, and nowhere informed the plaintiff that he had been diagnosed, or definitely diagnosed, with pancreatic cancer, neuroendocrine carcinomas, or “a cancer which is called the neuroendocrine cancer of the pancreas”; the defendants only highlighted the likelihood of PNETs and hyperplasia. [CITE:16]
- That advice also recorded that the current risk of spread or metastasis was not known, and that the uncinate lesion could represent a neuroendocrine tumour or hyperplasia. [CITE:16]
- The plaintiff’s own correspondence used the appropriate terminology: his email to Prof Ooi on 23 July 2010 was headed “Neuroendocrine tumours of the pancreas”, and when he sought clarification on 8 August 2010 about the Tumour Board’s differential reasoning, he never used the words “cancer”, “pancreatic cancer” or “neuroendocrine cancer”. [CITE:14] [CITE:16]
- The plaintiff accepted that he knew the difference between PNETs and pancreatic cancer, that he was not told explicitly that he had pancreatic cancer, and that his impression of cancer came from his own internet research and consultations with doctors in Malaysia. [CITE:5]
- He also never complained orally or in writing to either defendant soon after learning that the post-operative specimens showed no cancer or PNET, which the judge regarded as strongly indicating that no definitive diagnosis had ever been communicated to him. [CITE:3]
- Countervailing evidence: the plaintiff testified that the 13 August 2010 consultation was brief and that Prof Ooi said he would “carry out the surgery to remove both the cancerous lesions” in his pancreas. [CITE:8] The court nevertheless found, on the whole of the evidence including the contemporaneous emails, that the plaintiff had been informed of all the options and their advantages and disadvantages. [CITE:8]

## 2. The “surgery was the only option” claim was also rejected

- Dr Koo had earlier put three options to the plaintiff: octreotide treatment, radiopharmaceutical treatment, and surgery, with surgery described as “not unreasonable” rather than as the only course; radiopharmaceutical treatment was usually reserved for unresectable lesions, and octreotide would not achieve a cure if eradication were the objective. [CITE:4]
- The court found that Prof Ooi had made clear the surgical and non-surgical options and their implications, and that the plaintiff had been informed of all the various options open to him and the advantages and disadvantages of each. [CITE:8]
- Prof Ooi’s further advice included waiting six months for a repeat scan, removing only the body lesion or removing both lesions, and the higher morbidity and mortality of the Whipple Surgery compared with removal of the body lesion alone. [CITE:13] [CITE:18]
- The plaintiff was also advised that he could seek a second opinion from a private oncologist and surgeon, and he himself concluded that a negative EUS-FNA result would not significantly change the considerations for surgery because the uncinate lesion could still have been a PNET rather than hyperplasia. [CITE:17]
- The court found that he was cognisant of the clinical diagnosis and the differential diagnosis, that he had considered the risks of waiting six months, and that he decided on surgery after taking “all things considered” and choosing “option 2”, which was surgery. [CITE:9]

## 3. An important nuance in the court’s reasoning

- Counsel for Prof Ooi argued that “pancreatic cancer” should be read strictly as pancreatic exocrine adenocarcinomas and that the case run at trial therefore differed from the pleaded case; although the judge was prepared to accept that a PNET is not the same as pancreatic cancer, he held that this was not a sufficient basis to dispose of the allegation and instead examined the evidence directly to decide whether the plaintiff was ever actually informed or advised that he had pancreatic cancer. [CITE:12]
- The rejection therefore rests on the factual finding that no such statement was ever made, rather than on the narrower argument about terminology. [CITE:12]

## 4. Related findings on the pleaded allegations about the surgery itself

- The pleaded negligence allegations included a wrong diagnosis of pancreatic cancer, failure properly to consider the CT, MRI and blood test findings, failure to carry out a pre-operative EUS-FNA and intraoperative frozen section, and that the Whipple Surgery was not reasonably indicated and should have been aborted after a negative intraoperative ultrasound. [CITE:6]
- The court accepted the evidence that palpation of the pancreas was a good diagnostic tool in the absence of a positive intraoperative ultrasound, and that surgery on both lesions was logically indicated because pre-operative differentiation between PNETs and hyperplasia was not possible short of post-surgical histopathology; the EUS-FNA would not have supplied that missing information. [CITE:20] [CITE:1]
- The court also noted that the medical experts did not take apart the advice given to the plaintiff in order to argue that any one part of it was inappropriate or unreasonable. [CITE:11]

In short, the court rejected both limbs of the plaintiff’s case on the evidence, finding that he had been told of the possibility of hyperplasia as well as PNETs, had been offered several alternatives to surgery, and had chosen surgery after seeking and receiving clarifications. [CITE:7] [CITE:8] [CITE:9]

As at 2026-11-06, Ms Pai's claim failed on **causation**, not because the Court of Appeal disagreed that Dr Yeo fell short of the required standard of care.

## 1. What was in dispute

Ms Pai, a translation business owner, consulted Dr Yeo, a general practitioner, twice in December 1996 and claimed damages for negligence and/or breach of duty in respect of the loss of vision in her left eye caused by an internal eye infection. [CITE:2][CITE:6]

On 23 December 1996 she reported, for the first time, blurring of vision and spots in her left eye; Dr Yeo examined her, found the corneas clear and the pupils reacting normally, and suspected a detached retina as well as a urinary tract infection. [CITE:12][CITE:15][CITE:20]

The trial judge found that Dr Yeo fell short of the standard of care of a general practitioner because he did not advise her to go immediately to hospital or to an eye specialist in private practice, and held that she had complied with the advice given. [CITE:6][CITE:15]

Dr Yeo's appeal raised three contentions: that he did not breach the standard of care, that the breach did not cause the loss of vision, and that the loss was not foreseeable as a direct consequence of the breach. [CITE:8]

## 2. Why the breach point did not decide the case

A detached retina is an emergency requiring immediate attention by an eye specialist, and Dr Yeo accepted that any competent general practitioner would have advised the patient to go immediately to a hospital or consult an eye specialist that very afternoon. [CITE:1][CITE:3]

The trial judge had held that a GP is the patient's first line of defence for spotting illnesses requiring specialist or immediate attention, and that it was not fair to expect a GP to diagnose all urgent ailments accurately. [CITE:4]

Dr Yeo could not be faulted for failing to diagnose the actual condition, Endogenous Klebsiella Endophthalmitis (EKE), because the disease was so unusual that it would have been unreasonable to expect a GP to diagnose it. [CITE:3][CITE:4][CITE:19]

## 3. The decisive issue: causation was not proved

The Court of Appeal held that the **burden of proof rests squarely on Ms Pai**, and that she had not discharged it by showing, on the balance of probabilities, that had Dr Yeo advised her to go to the hospital or eye centre immediately on the afternoon of 23 December 1996 and had she gone there that afternoon, her left eye would have been saved. [CITE:11]

The Court found that the medical evidence was "far from convincing or conclusive" on that question. [CITE:11]

The Court also rejected the approach of transposing the events of 24 December back to 23 December, because the eye symptoms that appeared on 24 December were not present on 23 December, and because the Klebsiella bacteria grows at an exponential rate within 24 hours. [CITE:11]

## 4. Why the causation evidence was insufficient

The plaintiff's expert, Professor Cartwright, said it was not possible to give a precise answer because the extent of the eye involvement on 23 December was unknown, but that the earlier the infection was treated the greater the chance of success, and that if the infection was at an early stage on 23 December there was a possibility the eye could have been saved by immediate and appropriate treatment. [CITE:13]

Dr Ang, Dr Yeo's expert, conceded that it was possible, and more likely than not, that the eye would have been saved had she attended A&E at SGH on the evening of 23 December, but his opinion was expressly qualified by three conditions: that the correct diagnosis was made, that appropriate treatment was given, and that the eye responded to treatment. [CITE:18][CITE:20]

Dr Ang also gave evidence that a definitive diagnosis of internal endophthalmitis could only be made by culturing fluid taken from inside the eye, with laboratory results usually available 24 to 48 hours later, and that at the time of Dr Yeo's examination there was hardly any sign in the eye to suggest an internal infection. [CITE:19]

He further noted that early systemic treatment does not necessarily guarantee a good visual result because EKE can develop in patients already receiving intravenous antibiotics, that the prognosis is poor, and that the bacteria can destroy the eye very rapidly, sometimes within 24 hours. [CITE:19]

## 5. The "material contributory cause" test applied

Applying *Hotson v East Berkshire Area Health Authority*, the plaintiff had to prove on the balance of probabilities that the delayed treatment was at least a **material contributory cause** of the harm; unless she did so, she failed on causation and no question of quantification arose. [CITE:7][CITE:9]

In *Yeo*, the Court concluded that Ms Pai had not proved that Dr Yeo's negligence and/or breach of duty caused or materially contributed to the loss of her vision, and that her claim therefore could not succeed. [CITE:11]

## 6. Result

The Court of Appeal allowed Dr Yeo's appeal, set aside the judgment below and dismissed Ms Pai's claim because causation had not been established, and expressly declined to consider the issue of remoteness. [CITE:5]

In short, the claim failed because, although Dr Yeo breached his duty by not directing immediate specialist attention on 23 December 1996, the evidence did not satisfy the balance of probabilities that this breach was the cause of the permanent loss of her left eye. [CITE:3][CITE:11]
